extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (patent attorneys and agents) who practice before the United States Patent and Trademark Office
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and disciplinary benchmarks governing the professional responsibilities, office management, client communication, and docketing/calendar practices of attorneys and agents who practice patent (and related) matters before the USPTO. Drawn from a USPTO OED Final Order describing failures and required practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) (proscribing neglect of entrusted legal matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) proscribes neglect of entrusted legal matters. In this case, violation manifested by allowing patents to expire for not timely paying maintenance fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example failure: relying on an unsound manual docketing system that resulted in missed maintenance-fee payments and expired patents. Sanctionable conduct includes neglect that results in loss of client rights (e.g., patent expiration).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a) and (b) via 10.23(c)(8) (failing to inform a client of important Office correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must inform clients of important Office correspondence; failing to do so violates 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a) and (b) as applied via § 10.23(c)(8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example failures: not forwarding Notices of Patent Expiration or USPTO decisions to clients, not providing copies of petitions or decisions. Practitioners should have procedures to ensure important Office mail is identified and clients are promptly informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6) (conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10.23(b)(6) proscribes engaging in any other conduct that adversely reflects on a practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad standard captures behavior such as providing misleading information to clients, submitting filings without adequate inquiry, or allowing systemic office failures that harm clients' patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain adequate docketing system
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must maintain a reliable docketing system for recording, responding to, and otherwise keeping track of important Office correspondence and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: using a white board with limited retention, a single Word listing with no table/structure, no backup calendar, no automated tickler. Good practice: use an auditable, backed-up docketing system (ideally automated), print or archive records regularly, and ensure entries include attorney docket number, action type, due date, response taken, and response date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain adequate calendaring system and ensure compliance with Office deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must maintain an effective calendaring system to track and meet Office deadlines, including maintenance-fee payment deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calendar entries for maintenance fee due dates, surcharge deadlines, reconsideration/reply due dates. Do not rely solely on ephemeral displays (e.g., a white board) or single-person memory; implement backups and reminders to prevent missed deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate staffing relative to workload
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must staff their law offices adequately in light of the amount of patent work for which they are responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to hire additional staff when workload increases (creating undue stress on existing staff) is sanctionable if it causes neglect. Monitor workload, hire or redistribute tasks, and avoid overreliance on a single employee for critical functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper training, supervision, and monitoring of employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an obligation to properly train and supervise their employees and are responsible for the acts and omissions of their employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervision includes training, verifying work quality, establishing escalation procedures, creating a work environment where employees report problems, and taking steps if performance declines. The Office will consider whether the practitioner took steps to ensure an employee could handle increased workload without drop in quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward important Office correspondence to clients and keep clients informed
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must forward important Office correspondence to clients and inform clients promptly about material developments affecting their patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Notices of Patent Expiration, Office decisions denying petitions, and requests for reconsideration should be copied to clients; failure to provide copies or notice (or to respond to client inquiries accurately) is sanctionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct reasonable inquiry before signing and filing submissions with the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Before signing and filing submissions with the USPTO, a practitioner must conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances to verify the accuracy and basis of the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to investigate or verify facts (e.g., relying unquestioningly on an employee's statements or submitting declarations without substantiation) can violate professional obligations. This includes verifying file contents and the authenticity of evidence submitted under oath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain integrity and authenticity of documents submitted to the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents and exhibits submitted under oath to the USPTO must be authentic and truthful; altering or fabricating copies is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order discusses allegations that file-jacket copies were altered (handwritten notations added to photocopies) and submitted under oath. Practitioners must ensure that copies submitted are accurate representations of originals and must disclose if items have been modified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularly review and inventory files and docket reports to verify integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should perform regularly scheduled inventories of files and docket reports to verify their accuracy and integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: no scheduled inventory, reliance on a single list that is not periodically checked against physical files. Regular audits help detect missed deadlines, missing correspondence, or improper annotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely respond to Office decisions and docket response/reconsideration deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must docket and timely respond to Office decisions, including decisions on petitions and deadlines for requests for reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example failures: not docketing the due date to request reconsideration, not filing timely responses to a decision dismissing a petition. Maintain procedures to capture mailings from the Office and act within statutory or regulatory windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading communications to clients about patent status
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not give misleading or inaccurate information to clients concerning the status of their patents or pending actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order cites instances where the respondent gave misleading information about patent status. Best practice: verify status in USPTO records and provide copies of relevant Office actions when communicating with clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioners may be disciplined for employee violations resulting from inadequate supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered practitioners and others who practice before the Office may be disciplined when their employees have violated provisions of the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility because of a lack of adequate training or supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary exposure is not limited to the individual's own acts; failures in office management that permit employees to cause client harm can be an independent ground for discipline. Maintain supervision, spot-checks, and escalation protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use written engagement agreements to clarify responsibilities (recommended practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not expressly codified in the Order as a rule, the facts show that lack of written engagement agreements (e.g., who is responsible for maintenance-fee payments) contributed to confusion and client harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: use written engagement letters that state who will track and pay maintenance fees, which party is responsible for receiving Office correspondence, and what client notifications the firm will provide. Clear written agreements reduce ambiguity and can mitigate disputes.
